Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

issues.explanation: The trigger set suggests a highly specific external threat context involving cyclists and thrown objects, but the rest of the profile (memory and appraisals) does not contain corresponding content about that kind of event. In a man-made disaster profile, 'burnt smell' coheres with disaster-related sensory memory, whereas 'people cycling' and 'throwing objects' pull toward a different trauma scenario and are hard to integrate with the remaining items.

'Avoid seeing friends' is not well supported by the rest of the selected profile. The active formulation strongly links Triggers with Memory and Maladaptive Strategies, and the endorsed strategies are otherwise cognitive/internal (thought avoidance, thought monitoring). Social avoidance could occur in PTSD, but here it is not tied to any endorsed trigger, memory content, or appraisal pattern, making it look like a strategy for a different symptom cluster than the one described.

vignette:
David, a 55-year-old counselor living alone in a Midwestern city, still remembers the afternoon two years ago when a gas leak in his office building ignited without warning. He had been sitting with a client, discussing a routine issue, when the air turned sharp with the smell of natural gas, followed by a deafening blast. The concussion threw his desk chair against the wall; ceiling tiles and shards of glass rained down around him. He remembers the acrid, oily smell of smoke and something electrical burning, and the sight of a metal filing cabinet toppling and hurling a drawer across the room. He crawled out through a haze of dust and heat, coughing, his hands scraped, but physically unharmed. That day became a fault line in his life.

In the weeks that followed, certain smells could undo him without warning. The faint whiff of burnt toast in his own kitchen would send his heart pounding, and he would immediately push aside whatever he was doing—cancelling plans with friends, for instance, because the thought of being around other people felt unbearable. When he caught the scent of smoke from a neighbor’s fireplace, he felt the full emotional intensity of the explosion all over again, even though he could not always see a clear image in his mind—just a wave of dread and a racing pulse. The memory itself felt strangely foreign, as if it belonged to someone else, a story he had heard rather than lived. He came to believe that his body was betraying him: why else would it keep reacting as if he were still trapped in that room, even when he was safe at home? The conviction that his body was untrustworthy and out of control caused the memory of the explosion to surface more often, as though his mind kept checking to see if the danger was still real. He began to think he had to be constantly on guard, scanning every room for signs of gas or smoke, watching how people moved in case someone suddenly threw an object. He also became convinced that if he let himself think about the explosion in any detail, he would lose his grip entirely—so he tried to keep his mind deliberately blank, monitoring his own thoughts for any drift toward that day. Each time a memory surfaced, he would shut it down, and each time he shut it down, the memory felt more intrusive and less real the next time it came. Because the memory returned with such visceral force, ordinary sensations—the hiss of a radiator, the smell of a gas stove pilot light—began to feel like immediate threats, each one capable of pulling him back into the blast.

Over months, these reactions tightened into a cycle he could not escape. The slightest unexpected noise—a book dropped on a table, a door slammed—would trigger a full recall: the smell of smoke, the feeling of debris flying, and then the disconnected sense that none of it was actually happening to him. That feeling, in turn, confirmed his belief that he was going crazy, which only made him more vigilant, more watchful. At work, he found himself avoiding clients who brought up topics even remotely related to fires or disasters; during sessions he would catch himself scanning the room for exits rather than listening. He stopped seeing friends because he could not stand the thought of someone playfully tossing a shoe or a ball—any object thrown in the air sent him straight into that alien, fragmented memory. He knew his avoidance was making the memories stronger, but the alternative—letting them in—seemed too dangerous.

What finally brought him to therapy was an ordinary evening. He was walking home and smelled wood smoke from a backyard fire pit. Instantly his chest tightened, his mouth went dry, and he felt the full force of the explosion without any image—just that overwhelming terror. He stood frozen on the sidewalk, convinced that if he moved, he would fall apart. He realised then that he had stopped living. He still works as a counselor, but he goes through the motions mechanically, afraid of his own mind. He hopes to understand why his own body and memory feel like enemies, and to find a way back to a life that does not revolve around constant watchfulness and retreat.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not show a causal relationship where negative appraisals (e.g., beliefs about being betrayed by his body or going crazy) directly lead to the emergence of intrusive memories.
The vignette does not show that the trauma memory itself causes neutral stimuli to become triggers; instead, triggers consistently lead to memory.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not show a causal relationship where negative appraisals (e.g., beliefs about being betrayed by his body or going crazy) directly lead to the emergence of intrusive memories.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not show that the trauma memory itself causes neutral stimuli to become triggers; instead, triggers consistently lead to memory.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
